meanings.note: Manner/predicative adverb in '-о', derived from the neuter short form of the corresponding adjective.

examples.trans: Alright, Mom, I am very glad.

examples.text: Привет, девичник прошёл у вас хорошо?
examples.trans: Hi, did your bachelorette party go well?
Nikita is a very good person, after all.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'what, that', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: I do, and what does that mean?
Nastya, tell me, what should I do?
Wait, have we arrived already?

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'you (informal)', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: You will handle general supervision.
You look simply like a princess.
Just do not scare me.

meanings.en: to stand up, to get up (out of bed)
meanings.note: Prefix 'вс-' ('up') marks upward or sudden onset of action (stem 'тать'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'stood up, got up', paired with 'вставать'.

examples.text: У меня чуть сердце не встало!
examples.trans: My heart nearly stopped!
Lyova, it is good that you stood up.

examples.text: Кто первый встал, того и тапки.
examples.trans: First come, first served (whoever got up first gets the slippers).

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'I', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: С возвращением тебя к нам, Витя!
examples.trans: Welcome back to us, Vitya!
But a special thank you to my son-in-law.

examples.text: Папа, он пока ещё не зять.
examples.trans: Dad, he is not your son-in-law yet.

meanings.note: Prefix 'до-' marks reaching a boundary or finishing the remainder of an action (stem 'лжен'). Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('must').

examples.trans: There is no point in continuing the duel now.
We must ruin this wedding.
You must walk up to him.

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'делать'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'to do, to make', paired with 'делать'.

examples.text: В тот день он сделал предложение.
examples.trans: On that day he proposed to me.
Wait, did I really do that?
I must make an important announcement.

meanings.note: Adjective formed with the common Slavic suffix '-н-' from a noun/verb root. Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('important').

examples.trans: Wait, this is very important right now.
I must make an important announcement.
It's an important question.

meanings.note: Prefix 'за-' marks beginning an action, covering, or stopping by along the way (stem 'явление'). Verbal action/result neuter noun formed with '-ение'/'-ание'. Common neuter noun meaning 'statement' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: I must make an important announcement.
He wrote a statement.
Where is my application?

meanings.note: Manner/predicative adverb in '-о', derived from the neuter short form of the corresponding adjective.

examples.trans: They cook much better than you.
Do not drink too much here.
And there is too much cinnamon here.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian discourse particle adding conversational nuance meaning 'not', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Папа, он пока ещё не зять.
examples.trans: Dad, he is not your son-in-law yet.
Vitya, you must not get nervous at all.
I actually like this idea.

meanings.note: Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'work', paired with 'поработать'.

examples.trans: Heavy work is forbidden for you right now.
Only the best work in the kitchen!

examples.text: У тебя здесь работа и мама.
examples.trans: You have your work and mother here.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian spatial or relational preposition meaning 'for', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Misha, thank you for everything.
Heavy work is forbidden for you right now.

examples.text: Всю жизнь я за тебя боялась.
examples.trans: All my life I was afraid for you.

meanings.note: Borrowed from French 'restaurant' (from 'restaurer', to restore strength with rich broth); entered Russian in the early 19th century.

examples.trans: And change the name of the restaurant altogether!
Because this is my restaurant.
I am not worried about the restaurant.

meanings.note: Prefix 'пере-' denotes crossing over, repeating, or exceeding a limit (stem 'живать'). Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'worry', paired with 'пережить'.

examples.trans: Do not worry, everything will be fine.
I am not worried about the restaurant.
Why are you worrying like that?

meanings.note: Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('big').

examples.trans: And thank you all very much.
Thank you very much for reminding me.
Yes, I wish great happiness to you both.

meanings.note: Prefix 'про-' indicates movement through, completion, or missing the mark (stem 'фессионал'). Common masculine noun meaning 'professional' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: Lyova is a great professional and friend.
He's a real professional.
There's nothing but professionals here.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian clause-linking conjunction meaning 'and', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: С возвращением тебя к нам, Витя!
examples.trans: Welcome back to us, Vitya!
Misha, thank you for everything.
And thank you all very much.

meanings.note: Common masculine noun meaning 'friend' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: Did you understand me, my friend?
Is there no other place for a talk?
Lyova is a great professional and friend.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'he', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Папа, он пока ещё не зять.
examples.trans: Dad, he is not your son-in-law yet.
He brought his own team here.
Did he fire all of my cooks?

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'my', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Did you understand me, my friend?
Because this is my restaurant.
He is my very best friend.

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'амый'). Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('most').

examples.trans: Anywhere at all, choose for yourself.
Or we can steal Katya herself.
Just the thing for street dogs!

meanings.note: Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('best').

examples.trans: He fired the best cooks in Moscow.
They cook much better than you.
Only the best work in the kitchen!

meanings.note: Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'came', paired with 'приходить'.

examples.trans: Security will be here any moment.
I'll come tomorrow.

examples.text: Не надо, Самсон. Сейчас придёт охрана.
examples.trans: Don't, Samson. Security will be here any second.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian conversational adverb meaning 'it's time', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Chef, we will tear them apart today!
Everything is fine, let us go now.
I need to get to the airport urgently!

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'you', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: This is our new head chef.
He fired the best cooks in Moscow.
You look simply like a princess.

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'тать'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'to become', paired with 'становиться'.

examples.trans: Let us put my guys against yours.
Let us do it like in the old days!
Whoever cooks better will stay.

meanings.note: Prefix 'про-' indicates movement through, completion, or missing the mark (stem 'стить'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'forgive', paired with 'прощать'.

examples.trans: Chef, forgive me for the dish.
Forgive me, please, for everything.
Forgive me, our wedding is called off today.

meanings.note: Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'can, am able to', paired with 'смочь'.

examples.trans: I can't today.
That can't be.

examples.text: Этого не может быть. Это наша история.
examples.trans: That can't be. It's our history.

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'ейчас').

examples.trans: Heavy work is forbidden for you right now.
Believe me, right now it is not too late.

examples.text: Парни, сейчас всё в ваших руках.
examples.trans: Guys, everything is in your hands right now.

meanings.en: to fly away, to leave by plane
meanings.note: Prefix 'у-' marks departure, removal, or successful completion (stem 'летать'). Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'am flying away', paired with 'улететь'.

examples.trans: I am flying to Bishkek right now.
I am flying away, perhaps for five years.
I'm flying to Yerevan.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian spatial or relational preposition meaning 'in, into', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: С возвращением тебя к нам, Витя!
examples.trans: Welcome back to us, Vitya!
Misha, thank you for everything.
And thank you all very much.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian conversational adverb meaning 'maybe', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: I am allowed, I am not the groom.
We can steal her wedding dress.
Or we can steal Katya herself.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian spatial or relational preposition meaning 'on, onto', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: С возвращением тебя к нам, Витя!
examples.trans: Welcome back to us, Vitya!
Let us go to the kitchen quickly.
I want to look at my cooks.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian cardinal or ordinal numeral meaning 'five', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Denis, is that you in here again?

examples.text: В Москву приедет через пять лет.
examples.trans: She will come to Moscow in five years.
I am flying away, perhaps for five years.

meanings.note: Common masculine noun meaning 'years' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: Let us hold a fair duel today.
Let us leave here together today.
Anywhere at all, choose for yourself.

meanings.note: Prefix 'из-' ('out from within') marks extraction or exhaustion (stem 'винить'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'excuse me', paired with 'извинять'.

examples.trans: Excuse me for this decision.
Sorry, I'm in a hurry.
Sorry, please.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'this, it (is)', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: That title will be his in twenty-four hours.
This is our new head chef.
Really, and who is this man?

meanings.note: Verbal action/result neuter noun formed with '-ение'/'-ание'. Common neuter noun meaning 'decision, ruling, solution' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: Excuse me for this decision.
I am forced to cancel my decision.
This is the right decision.

meanings.note: Prefix 'на-' marks surface contact, accumulation, or completing a quantity (stem 'стоящий'). Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('true').

examples.trans: You have a real circus in here!
Viktor Petrovich, this is true love.
This is real success!

meanings.note: Common feminine noun meaning 'love' in everyday Russian.

examples.text: Женщина может уйти в любой момент.
examples.trans: A woman can leave at any moment.
Viktor Petrovich, this is true love.
Run after your love!

meanings.en: to run (in one direction), to flee, to escape
meanings.note: Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'run', paired with 'побежать'.

examples.trans: Lyova, where are you running off to now?
That is it, I am running off to the bachelorette party.
Your daughter just ran away from the altar.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'your, one's own', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: I want to look at my cooks.
He brought his own team here.
Go and win back your jobs.
